claims.text: Standard-dose second-generation H1 antihistamines are first-line treatment for uncomplicated hives
claims.quote: We recommend the use of a standard‐dosed modern 2nd generation H‐antihistamines as the first‐line symptomatic treatment for urticaria.

claims.text: No single best antihistamine; cetirizine and fexofenadine are examples with urticaria evidence
claims.quote: no recommendation can be made on which to choose because, to date, well‐designed clinical trials directly comparing the efficacy and safety of all modern 2nd generation H‐antihistamines in urticaria are largely lacking.

claims.text: Cetirizine and fexofenadine are second-generation antihistamines supported for urticaria
claims.quote: evidence supports the use of bilastine, cetirizine, desloratadine, ebastine, fexofenadine, levocetirizine, loratadine, mizolastine, and rupatadine

claims.text: Up to fourfold up-dosing is for patients with insufficient response to a standard dose, preferred over mixing antihistamines
claims.quote: some patients with urticaria, who show insufficient response to a licensed‐dose of 2nd generation H‐antihistamine, benefit from updosing, which is preferred over mixing different 2nd generation H‐antihistamines since their pharmacologic properties are different.

claims.text: Up-dosing up to fourfold is off-label
claims.quote: We, therefore, recommend to increase the dose up to fourfold, in such patients (Figure). Patients need to be informed that 2nd generation H‐antihistamine updosing is off‐label

claims.text: Short oral steroid course of no more than 10 days may help in acute urticaria or a flare
claims.quote: For acute urticaria and acute exacerbations of CSU, a short course of oral corticosteroids, that is, treatment of a maximum of up to 10 days, may, however, be helpful to reduce disease duration/activity

claims.text: Well-designed trials of short steroid courses are lacking
claims.quote: Nevertheless, well‐designed randomized clinical trials are lacking.

claims.text: Guideline strongly recommends against prolonged systemic steroids
claims.quote: we strongly recommend against the prolonged use of corticosteroids.

claims.text: Acute urticaria lasts up to 6 weeks
claims.quote: is defined as the occurrence of wheals, angioedema or both for 6 weeks or less.

claims.text: Hives beyond 6 weeks are chronic urticaria and need reassessment
claims.quote: is defined as the occurrence of wheals, angioedema, or both for more than 6 weeks.

claims.text: Wheals can merge into large areas
claims.quote: Intense (> 50 wheals/24 h or large confluent areas of wheals)

claims.text: Swelling without wheals, and persistent, bruised or blistering eruptions, may be another condition (e.g. bradykinin-mediated angioedema, urticarial vasculitis)
claims.quote: Urticaria needs to be differentiated from other medical conditions where wheals, angioedema, or both can occur as features of a spectrum of clinical conditions such as anaphylaxis, autoinflammatory syndromes, urticarial vasculitis, or bradykinin‐mediated angioedema

claims.text: A recent respiratory infection can precede hives
claims.quote: Acute urticaria frequently follows upper airways infections [], including COVID‐19 []

claims.text: Medicines and NSAIDs can cause hives; tell the clinician about pain relievers
claims.quote: Medications can lead to urticarial drug reactions with wheals occurring directly after intake

claims.text: Do not deliberately re-expose yourself to a suspected trigger
claims.quote: Patient education may also be useful to allow patients to avoid re‐exposure to the relevant causative factors.

claims.text: Repeated reactions to a predictable physical stimulus may indicate inducible urticaria
claims.quote: Inducible urticaria is characterized by the presence of definite and subtype‐specific triggers leading to the development of wheals, angioedema, or both []

claims.text: Stress can aggravate hives
claims.quote: It is evident that stress can exacerbate CSU, with up to one‐third of CSU patients perceiving stress as an aggravating factor

claims.text: No routine tests for acute spontaneous urticaria; history usually enough except suspected food or drug allergy
claims.quote: Acute urticaria, because of its self‐limiting nature, usually does not require a diagnostic workup beyond a thorough medical history aimed at identifying possible trigger factors, such as recent infections at the time of onset (e.g., a common cold).

claims.text: Exception for suspected food allergy or drug reaction
claims.quote: The only exception to this is the suspicion of an acute urticaria due to a food allergy in sensitized patients, or drug hypersensitivity, especially for nonsteroidal anti‐inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs).

claims.text: Avoid broad diets and supplement stacks; uncertainty is not a reason for extensive elimination diet
claims.quote: Importantly, the overdiagnosis of “histamine intolerance” should be avoided, as can lead to unnecessary dietary restrictions and misuse of commercial supplements.

claims.text: Medically necessary NSAID or aspirin use needs an individualized plan rather than stopping on your own
claims.quote: to find safe alternatives or tolerable doses in patients that use chronic NSAIDs due to other chronic medical conditions (i.e., coronary artery disease, rheumatoid arthritis)

claims.text: Topical steroids are not useful in urticaria
claims.quote: topical corticosteroids are frequently and successfully used in many allergic diseases, but are not useful in urticaria

claims.text: Newer antihistamines preferred over first-generation agents such as diphenhydramine
claims.quote: we recommend against their use for the routine management of CU as first‐line agents

claims.text: Bring time-stamped photos
claims.quote: it is important to review prior documentation, including patient‐provided photographs of wheals and/or angioedema

claims.text: Treatment is adjusted to response; recurrent disease follows a stepwise plan with continuity
claims.quote: stepping up or stepping down in the treatment algorithm according to the course of disease

claims.text: Newer antihistamines are first-line for urticaria and preferred over first-generation agents for safety
claims.quote: Second- and third-generation AHs are the recommended first-line treatment for mild allergic rhinitis and acute and chronic urticaria.

claims.text: Diphenhydramine side effects: sedation, dry mouth, dizziness, impaired cognition
claims.quote: Older, first-generation AHs (e.g. diphenhydramine, hydroxyzine) have significant and common side effects including sedation, impairment with decreased cognitive function, poor sleep quality, dry mouth, dizziness, and orthostatic hypotension.

claims.text: Impaired attention with first-generation antihistamines
claims.quote: next-day “hang-over” effects like impaired vigilance, divided attention, working memory, sensory-motor performance, and reduced latency to daytime sleep has been observed

claims.text: Do not use a sedating antihistamine as a sleep aid; older agents do not produce quality sleep
claims.quote: Despite their sedative effects, these older medications do not result in quality sleep

claims.text: 'Non-drowsy' does not guarantee zero impairment; sedation varies by drug and dose
claims.quote: The level of sedation experienced by patients taking newer generation AHs varies by specific medication and the dose.

claims.text: Diphenhydramine is not a replacement for epinephrine in anaphylaxis
claims.quote: Epinephrine is the drug of choice for anaphylaxis, but H1-antihistamines are also used in its treatment

claims.text: Antihistamines block histamine signaling that produces wheals and itch
claims.quote: Histamine is a biogenic amine whose release results in allergic rhino-conjunctival symptoms as well as the urticarial wheal and flare reaction with itch

claims.text: Heat, pressure, cold and scratching can provoke inducible hives
